# Letting AI Formulate the Research Question: Autonomous Research Agents

Ko Fujimura ^(†)^(†)thanks: fujimura@otsuma.ac.jp Affiliation: Otsuma
Women’s University, Faculty of Social Information Studies

29 October 2026

###### Abstract

Systems such as The AI Scientist have shown that AI agents can carry out
and write up research, but in those demonstrations humans chose the
research area and selected the outputs to show. We study letting the AI
formulate the research question itself, and we report every run. Our
system gives an off-the-shelf coding agent an instruction document and
two skills: one for formulating the question, in which the agent
diverges from recent technologies into problems of other fields, screens
its candidates for known failure modes and obtains a critique from a
different model; and one for peer review, in which a reviewer from
another model family re-runs the study from its records before the agent
revises the paper. Over 13 development runs, changes to the one or two
sentences that set the research area coincided with large shifts in what
the candidate questions and the chosen papers were about, which led us
to the area of a new technology applied to a societal problem. We froze
the system after a pilot run and report five consecutive runs: the
pilot, counted by a disclosed amendment to the pre-registration, and
four pre-registered runs. All five runs went from question formulation
to a revised, re-computable paper, with local computation on a laptop
and no research input from humans, and external AI reviewers reading
only the papers judged them at or near workshop level. We release the
system, the five papers and the records needed to reproduce them.

## 1 Introduction

Automating research end to end has moved from aspiration to
demonstration. The AI Scientist \[[6](#bib.bib6)\] generated
machine-learning papers from code templates; The AI Scientist-v2
\[[19](#bib.bib19)\] removed the templates, added an agentic tree search
over experiments, and had one of three generated papers reach an
above-threshold score at an ICLR 2025 workshop; a later journal version
describes the full pipeline and an automated reviewer
\[[7](#bib.bib7)\]. Other systems automate parts of the process or
target particular sciences \[[13](#bib.bib13), [12](#bib.bib12),
[5](#bib.bib5), [9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10), [18](#bib.bib18)\],
and a venue has accepted papers with AI first authors
\[[2](#bib.bib2)\].

In these demonstrations a human still decides two things. The human
chooses _where_ to look: The AI Scientist works “within a user-specified
machine learning research subfield” \[[7](#bib.bib7)\], Jr. AI Scientist
starts from a given baseline paper \[[10](#bib.bib10)\], and the AI
co-scientist answers research goals set by scientists
\[[5](#bib.bib5)\]. The human also chooses _what to show_: the authors
of The AI Scientist-v2 “selected the most promising complete output” for
submission \[[19](#bib.bib19)\]. Within these bounds the systems
generate ideas and hypotheses themselves, but the frame in which a
question is formed, and the choice of which results are seen, remain
with people. We therefore separate three decisions: setting the research
area, formulating and selecting a specific question, and selecting which
outputs to report.

We ask what happens when the area is set only broadly, the specific
question is left to the AI, and nothing is filtered. The human sets the
area in one or two sentences (here, societal problems that can be
studied with open data); the agent writes its own candidate questions
and selects one, with no human selection; and every run is reported. Our
system is deliberately plain: a general-purpose coding agent, an
instruction document, and two skills (structured instructions loaded on
demand), with no bespoke orchestration code or experiment templates. The
research-question skill is a procedure for formulating questions that
targets failure modes we observed while developing the system: questions
whose answer follows from definitions, technologies used as decoration,
and questions with no public ground truth. A different model critiques
the top candidates once, and a reviewer from another model family
re-runs the study from its records before the agent revises the paper.

We froze the system after a pilot run and report five consecutive runs:
the pilot and four pre-registered runs. The pilot was counted by an
amendment made after three of the later results had been seen, which we
report as a deviation
(Section [5](#S5 "5 Evaluation design ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents")).
Our contributions are:

1.  1.  Autonomy without research intervention. All five runs completed
        question formulation, experiments, writing, AI review and revision,
        with local computation on a laptop. The records contain no research
        advice and no permission requests; the only inputs after the start
        were fixed messages to resume after usage limits and to relay the
        review
        (Section [6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Completion and inputs ‣ 6 Results ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents")).
2.  2.  Setting the research area. Over 13 development runs, changes to the
        sentences of the instructions that set the area coincided with large
        shifts in what the candidate questions and the chosen papers were
        about. We describe the path to the technology $`\times`$
        societal-problem setting and argue that more specific settings could
        yield correspondingly specific themes
        (Section [4](#S4 "4 Setting the research area: lessons from 13 development runs ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents")).
3.  3.  A procedure for formulating research questions and what it produced:
        77 candidate questions across nine societal fields, and the reasons
        candidates were discarded
        (Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Questions the agents formulated ‣ 6 Results ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents")).
4.  4.  Cross-model critique and review inside the loop. The critic changed
        how the chosen question was compared and measured in every run, and
        the reviewer re-computed every first draft and found problems of
        interpretation that the agent then fixed
        (Sections [6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 What the critique changed ‣ 6 Results ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents")–[6.4](#S6.SS4 "6.4 In-loop review and revision ‣ 6 Results ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents")).
5.  5.  An external AI evaluation of the five final papers by reviewers from
        two further model families
        (Section [6.6](#S6.SS6 "6.6 External AI evaluation ‣ 6 Results ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents")),
        and the release of the system, the papers and the records.

## 2 Related work

#### End-to-end research systems.

The AI Scientist \[[6](#bib.bib6)\] introduced a pipeline of idea
generation, code edits on a template, experiments, write-up and
automated review. The AI Scientist-v2 \[[19](#bib.bib19)\] added
template-free experimentation with a tree search managed by an
experiment-manager agent and was evaluated by submitting three papers to
a workshop; the journal version \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] reports that paper
quality, as judged by its automated reviewer, improves with newer
foundation models and more test-time compute. Agent Laboratory
\[[13](#bib.bib13)\] and AgentRxiv \[[12](#bib.bib12)\] use LLM agents
as research assistants with human input at chosen points; Jr. AI
Scientist \[[10](#bib.bib10)\] extends a given baseline paper and
reports the risks it observed; Kosmos \[[9](#bib.bib9)\] and Denario
\[[18](#bib.bib18)\] target data-driven discovery; the AI co-scientist
\[[5](#bib.bib5)\] generates and ranks hypotheses for scientists. Trehan
and Chopra \[[17](#bib.bib17)\] describe four autonomous research
attempts and their failure modes. Closest to our setting, the
Scientist-Bench of AI-Researcher \[[16](#bib.bib16)\] includes
open-ended tasks in which the agent must find its own research direction
from given reference papers and datasets. Luo et al. \[[8](#bib.bib8)\]
show that failures such as inappropriate benchmark selection, data
leakage, metric misuse and post-hoc selection are detected far more
effectively from workflow logs and code than from the final paper alone.
Our system differs in that it contains no bespoke orchestration code,
sets the area only broadly instead of giving a subfield, baseline, goal
or reference papers, and does not filter outputs; the records that allow
re-computation are part of its product.

#### Research ideation by LLMs.

In a large human study, LLM-generated research ideas were judged more
novel but slightly less feasible than those of experts
\[[14](#bib.bib14)\]; when the ideas were executed, the advantage
disappeared \[[15](#bib.bib15)\]. An independent evaluation of The AI
Scientist found weak literature review and frequent experiment failures
\[[1](#bib.bib1)\]. A recent study asks whether an agentic workflow can
propose research questions that experts in mathematics, statistics,
theoretical computer science and physics find interesting
\[[11](#bib.bib11)\]. We observe question formulation inside complete,
unfiltered research runs, together with the critiques and reviews that
followed.

## 3 System

### 3.1 Roles

A run involves a human and four agents
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents")).
We describe them in the order in which they act; the numbers refer to
the steps in the figure.

The human organises the study. The human approves the instructions for
each run, sets the API key in the terminal used for research and hands
that terminal to the management agent (steps 1–2), and would decide any
permission request; there were none in the evaluation runs.

The management agent is Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 in a separate
workspace. It fills in the instructions for each run (1), starts the
research session with them (3), resumes the session after usage limits
with fixed messages (6), starts the reviewer once the first draft is
tagged (7), and relays the review verbatim (10). After the run it reads
the final paper and records (11), notifies the human (12) and writes a
post-run assessment (13). It sends no research advice, and nothing it
writes other than the instructions is visible to the research session.
During development these assessments led to the next version of the
instructions; during the evaluation runs the instructions were frozen.

The research agent is Codex CLI with gpt-6.1-sol (reasoning effort
xhigh), started in a dedicated directory with the instruction document
as its first message. It formulates the question, carries out the study
and writes the paper, using its tools, web search and local computation.
Through an API it may call one other model, the critic, within a budget
of US\$20.

The critic is gpt-6-astra (reasoning effort xhigh, with web search). The
research agent sends it its top five candidate questions without its
scores or ranking (4) and receives one critique (5). Whether to adopt
each point is the research agent’s decision.

The reviewer is Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 (effort xhigh), without
API keys. It works on a copy of the tagged draft and its records (8),
re-runs the study through its verification entry point, checks that
plans precede results, searches for prior work, and writes a review with
a verdict, six scores and numbered findings (9). The research agent then
has two hours to respond and submit the final version.

### 3.2 Instructions and skills

The instruction document (about 7,300 English words) states that the
human will not specify the content, that negative results and failures
are to be submitted as they are, and that the resource limits are for
scoping a chosen question, not a source of ideas. It sets the conditions
(12 hours to the draft and 2 hours for the review response, excluding
usage-limit stops; 10 GiB of storage; at most two concurrent experiments
of up to 30 minutes each), the records to keep, the rules on security,
privacy and data about people, and a hint toward societal problems that
can be studied with open data. It does not name a field or a topic.

The research-question skill (about 2,400 words) is the procedure for
formulating the question:

1.  1.  Record the first three candidates that come to mind as _obvious
        candidates_; they may be adopted, but their non-obviousness score is
        at most 2.
2.  2.  _Diverge from technologies_: list at least six technologies from
        different subfields of computer science that first became possible
        around 2024 or later, each confirmed by a source; generalise each
        into capabilities without its name; for each capability, find fields
        outside computer science where someone could not make a judgment
        because of the removed constraint; check for public data; and write
        at least twelve questions, with no technology or field supplying
        more than a third of them and no type of study more than half.
3.  3.  Check each question against six points: whether the study is
        possible without the capability (decoration); whether the technology
        or an existing method has already been applied to the same problem;
        whether the main result follows from definitions or how the data are
        produced; whether AI judgments in it can be checked against public
        ground truth; whether the technology or its published outputs can be
        used here; and which decision changes in which direction for each
        possible answer. A candidate that fails one of the first four checks
        is revised or discarded; one that fails the fifth or sixth is
        discarded.
4.  4.  Check prior work for the top five, run short feasibility probes for
        the top three, and score every candidate from 1 to 5 on seven axes
        (impact, novelty, non-obviousness, generality, unpredictability,
        feasibility, strength of verification), with a one-line reason for
        each.
5.  5.  Obtain one critique of the top five from the critic, sending only
        the questions, method outlines and closest prior work (not the
        scores or the preferred candidate); verify any prior work it cites;
        classify each point as adopted or not, with reasons; and re-score if
        needed, keeping the original scores. Rankings or new topics proposed
        by the critic may not be used as grounds for adopting or rejecting a
        candidate.
6.  6.  Select by the total of impact, novelty, non-obviousness, generality
        and unpredictability; a candidate with feasibility 2 or less is
        first narrowed and re-scored. Write a pre-mortem (the one-sentence
        claim if it succeeds, the three likely first objections and the
        responses), and run a safety check.

The skill also lists types of study to avoid, such as quantitative
re-confirmation of a known concern and applying an existing measurement
to a new target only. The checks and scores are the agent’s own
judgments, recorded with reasons; nothing enforces them.

The peer-review skill (about 1,800 words) tells the reviewer to record
its prior expectation from the title and research question, to re-run
the verification steps on a copy of the tagged commit without calling AI
APIs, to check the timeline of plans and results, the evidence for each
claim, the cited and the missing prior work, and to write the report. A
separate review instruction (about 1,600 words) starts the reviewer.

### 3.3 Run records and operation

The research agent keeps the records of its run in its directory, under
version control. They are append-only and consist of:

- •
  plans and topic-selection records, committed before the experiments
  that use them;
- •
  a timeline of events, and every input from the human or the management
  agent, by type;
- •
  each claim with its evidence and whether it is exploratory;
- •
  each API call with its request, response and cost;
- •
  an environment manifest with the deadlines;
- •
  Git tags for the first draft and the final version, and a SHA-256 list
  of the files;
- •
  a single verification entry point that regenerates the reported
  numbers, tables and figures without AI calls.

These records are what the reviewer checks (step 8) and what the
management agent reads after the run (step 11). Research sessions use a
configuration directory separate from the human’s, so that the human’s
own skills, memories and earlier conversations are not visible; the
research workspace contains no evaluations of earlier runs, and the
instructions forbid reading earlier run directories, which were not
blocked by access control. Usage-limit stops of the subscription-based
agent are excluded from the time budget. All local computation ran on
one MacBook Pro (M3 Pro, 18 GiB of memory, no discrete GPU); the
language models were used as hosted services.

what the version of the instructions said about where to look;
“unchanged” refers to this part only, since other parts of the

Formulating the research question starts from where to look, and this
part of the instructions is the one we changed most. The system was
developed over 13 runs with Japanese instructions; between runs we
changed only the instructions and recorded the reason for each change.
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Setting the research area: lessons from 13 development runs ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents")
lists, for each run, what the instructions said about the research area,
the candidates the agent wrote, and the study it chose. These are
observations, not controlled comparisons: the research model, its
environment and other parts of the instructions also changed, and the
classification of the candidates is ours.

#### No area.

The first run had no field and no selection procedure. The agent listed
two candidates, chose an exact comparison in a classical probability
problem, and finished in about 12 minutes of its three-hour limit.

#### Computer science.

From run 002 to run 010 the instructions set the field to computer
science. The chosen studies stayed inside computer systems and AI
tooling: caches (runs 002 and 010), the edit tools of coding agents
(004), structured-generation engines (005) and document retrieval (009).
In run 010, 7 of the 15 candidates concerned compression, storage,
caching or deduplication, which are the kinds of constraint the
instructions imposed on the run itself; the agent appeared to derive its
topics from its own working conditions.

#### Single sentences and the agenda.

Within computer science, changes to single sentences coincided with
changes in what the candidates were about. When the instructions
welcomed “problems of the AI era” and scored candidates on that axis
(v1.2), most candidates concerned AI or AI tooling for both Claude
Opus 5.5 (9 of 16) and GPT-6 (8 of 11), and both runs chose AI tooling.
When the readers were set to be future autonomous research agents
(v1.3), Opus wrote mostly candidates about the behaviour of LLMs and
about research practice (16 of 19 and 15 of 18 in runs 006 and 007) and
chose one of them. When the readers were changed to researchers and
practitioners of the field (v1.6), the next run of gpt-6.1-sol wrote no
candidate about AI or research practice (the previous run of the same
model wrote four) and 11 about computer systems. Conversely, when the
area setting and the selection procedure were left almost unchanged
(v1.7 mainly changed how to write the paper and added a search for
classic prior work), run 010 repeated many of run 009’s candidates
(seven pairs by our matching), although neither run could see the other.

#### Societal problems.

In v1.8 we removed the field and added one sentence: “The research field
is not restricted. Freely devise research on themes such as discovering
societal problems using open data and other information on the Internet,
or proposing tools that help solve societal problems.” The version also
told the agent not to derive topics from the run’s resource limits and
named as readers those who work on the problem. With the same model and
environment as runs 009 and 010, 14 of 15 candidates concerned societal
problems (disasters and water, environment, energy, food, health and
official statistics), none corresponded to a candidate of the two
previous runs, and the chosen study moved from workflow caches to the
monitoring of PFAS in drinking water. This was not more freedom but a
different area: we did not test removing the field without adding the
hint.

#### Technology $`\times`$ societal problem.

The candidates were still written from memory, and with the same model
and procedure they repeated. In v1.9 we therefore made the divergence
start from technologies: list at least six technologies of computer
science that came into practical use in 2024 or later, generalise each
into capabilities, and look for fields outside computer science where
someone could not make a judgment because of the constraint that the
capability removes
(Section [3](#S3 "3 System ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents")).
Combined with the hint of v1.8, this sets the area that the evaluation
runs used: a new technology applied to a societal problem. Both research
models then wrote almost only societal candidates (15 of 17 with
gpt-6.1-sol in run 012, 15 of 15 with Claude Opus 5.5 in run 013). The
model changed the country and the subject rather than the area: 14 of
the 15 candidates of run 013 used Japanese institutions and data, while
the gpt-6.1-sol runs used none. Both chosen studies, however, used a
known kind of technology (machine translation in run 013) or an existing
application (a time-series forecaster already used for wastewater
surveillance in run 012). The English version used in the evaluation
therefore restricts the starting technologies to capabilities that first
became possible around 2024 or later, excluding new versions of an
existing kind of technology, and checks whether the technology has
already been applied to the same problem.

#### The checks.

The six checks came with the technology-first divergence. The check that
the main result does not follow from definitions or from how the data
are produced answers the most frequent leading finding of the
development reviews. The checks for decoration and for public ground
truth guard against using a new technology without need or without a way
to verify its judgments. In six short trials of the procedure that
stopped once the candidates were written (not counted as runs), the new
divergence lowered the rated feasibility of the candidates, so we added
the checks that the technology or its published outputs can be used in
the run’s environment and that each possible answer changes a decision
of the people who use the result. For the evaluation we translated the
instructions into English, split the question and review procedures into
skills, and froze them.

#### What this suggests.

Changes to the area setting coincided with the largest shifts in the
candidates that we observed, and with entirely different chosen papers;
the rest of the procedure acted within the area, on how well the
question was formed. Their effects were not isolated from the other
changes made at the same time. Because a one-sentence hint coincided
with a shift of 14 of 15 candidates, we expect that a more specific
setting, such as a particular field, problem, dataset or the open
decision of a particular user, would let the same procedure produce
correspondingly specific research themes while still leaving the
question itself to the agent. We have not tested this. The evaluation
runs also show the price of a fixed setting: within technology
$`\times`$ societal problems, the agents converged on a few
well-documented resources
(Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Questions the agents formulated ‣ 6 Results ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents")).

## 5 Evaluation design

We first ran a pilot (run 014) with the English instructions and, after
seeing its result, froze the system without changing it. We then
pre-registered the evaluation: the system (SHA-256 of every file), the
models and settings, the time and resource limits, the inclusion rules
(every run whose start message is sent is reported; no run is excluded
or repeated after its result is seen), and five counted runs, 015 to
019, excluding the pilot. After runs 015–017 had finished and their
results had been seen, and before run 018 started, we amended the plan
to count the pilot as the first run, because its filled instructions,
skills, models and settings were identical to those of the later runs
(verified by re-deploying the frozen files and comparing them); run 019
was therefore not made. The amendment added a run whose result had been
seen and ended the series one run early, so we report it as a deviation.
The pilot also differed in that the research workspace contained no
earlier runs. Versions v1.10 to v1.10.4 differ only in the version label
and the run number.

We report, for each run, the times, stops and inputs from the run
records and the management records; the candidates and their fates; the
critique and the agent’s decisions on each point; and the in-loop review
and the agent’s response. All numbers in the tables are generated by a
script from these records.

#### External AI evaluation (E1).

The pre-registration required re-review by AI reviewers from at least
two model families other than the researcher’s. Before sending any
review, we fixed the prompt, the output schema and the scripts. Two
reviewers, Gemini 4 Argon (thinking level high, Google Search tool) and
Muse Wonder (reasoning effort max, web-search tool), each reviewed each
final paper twice in independent requests. They saw only the paper and
could search the web; they were not given the code, data or records.
They were told that the paper was produced by an autonomous AI research
system. They scored the six axes of our review instructions, gave a
verdict, an overall score on the ICLR scale (1–10) as a full paper at a
strong venue in the paper’s own field, judgments of whether the paper
would be accepted at a workshop in its field (acceptance rate about 70%)
and at the main track of a top venue in its field (about 25–30%), and
rated the research question. These are uncalibrated AI assessments of
the papers alone, not calibrated against human decisions, and the 20
reviews are repeated assessments of five papers. The five papers are
published as PDFs; Gemini first reviewed the Markdown sources, and after
that we decided to review the PDFs, which are the published form, with
both reviewers. We report the PDF reviews as the main result and the
Markdown reviews in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A External AI evaluation of the Markdown sources ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents");
this choice was made after the Markdown results had been seen.

Table 2: Time and inputs. “Topic” is minutes from start to topic
selection (excluding stops); “Draft”, “Stops” and “Active” are
hours:minutes from start to the draft tag, of usage-limit stops, and
their difference; “Margin” is the time left before the draft deadline
(12 h plus stops). “Resumes” counts fixed resumption messages after
usage limits + after other stops. “Perm.” are permission requests and
“Advice” research-content inputs recorded in the run’s intervention log.
“Review” and “Resp.” are minutes of the AI review and of the agent’s
response. “API” is the cost of the critique in US dollars, as recorded
by the agent; in run 017 the agent recorded a range because it could not
determine how long cached input was retained. Times are rounded from
seconds, so Active may differ from Draft minus Stops by one minute.

All five runs produced a first draft within the time limit, completed
the AI review, and submitted a revised final version within the response
period
(Table [2](#S6.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 6.1 Completion and inputs ‣ 6 Results ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents")).
The intervention logs record no research advice and no permission
requests. After each start message, the research session received only
fixed messages from the management agent: 12 resumptions after usage
limits, 2 after other stops (the model was temporarily at capacity) and
5 review relays. The human set the API key and opened the terminal and
took no other action in the runs. The agents worked for 6.5 to 11.7
active hours before the draft; usage-limit stops added up to 6.3 hours
of waiting in one run. Each run made exactly one critique call, costing
about US\$2.

The records were not free of errors. In three runs, after the agent’s
conversation was automatically compacted, the agent took a resumption
message it had already answered for a new one and extended its own
deadline by up to 260 seconds; in run 018 it noticed and withdrew the
extra entry itself. We use the management records for all times.

| Run | Cand. | Tech. | Points | Adopted | On chosen |
| --- | ----- | ----- | ------ | ------- | --------- |
| 014 | 15    | 6     | 26     | 22      | 9         |
| 015 | 15    | 6     | 26     | 21      | 7         |
| 016 | 15    | 6     | 23     | 13      | 7         |

Table 4: Candidate questions and the critique. “Cand.” is the number of
candidates (3 obvious + 12–14 from the divergence), “Tech.” the number
of technologies listed in the divergence; “Points” the critic’s points
on the top five, “Adopted” those adopted or partly adopted by the agent,
and “On chosen” the points on the candidate that was finally chosen. In
no run did the critique change which candidate was chosen.

Table [3](#S6.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 6.2 Questions the agents formulated ‣ 6 Results ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents")
lists the questions. All five are societal or environmental questions
answered with public data and published model outputs: whether annual
satellite embeddings can screen tree-cover change, how much published
ensemble summaries constrain the probability that several places exceed
a temperature threshold together, how to re-sample reference locations
to estimate change in crop diversity, how the allocation of training
points affects the recovery of small wetlands in a map, and whether
embedding distances add to physical covariates when matching wetlands
with similar water regimes. None of the five is about AI itself; four
use annual satellite embeddings (AlphaEarth Foundations
\[[3](#bib.bib3)\] and TESSERA \[[4](#bib.bib4)\]), which became
available in 2025, as one of the objects of study rather than as
decoration, and one uses ensemble weather forecasts. Run 015 is a
boundary case of the requirement that a question depend on a newly
possible capability: its selection record states that the mathematical
question could have been studied before 2024 and that the new capability
(cheap ensemble forecasts from AI weather models) supplies the
motivation and a second class of real forecasts. The agent kept the
candidate, as its own judgment of the checks allowed.

The agents wrote 77 candidate questions
(Table [4](#S6.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 6.2 Questions the agents formulated ‣ 6 Results ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents");
counted per run, and similar candidates recur across runs). By our
classification, with one field per candidate, all 77 concern society or
the environment, in nine fields: environment (17), disaster and water
(14), food and agriculture (12), health (7), transport and welfare (7),
resources and materials (7), public administration (6), energy (4) and
cultural heritage (3). None concerns AI or research practice, and none
uses Japanese data. Topic selection took 33 to 72 minutes.

Most candidates were discarded for reasons that the six checks target:
the technology or its outputs could not be used here (for example, the
archive of a weather model’s forecasts required an access approval, and
the weights of a sound-separation model were gated), there was no public
ground truth for the decision of interest, the result followed from a
threshold definition, or close prior work already covered it. In run
018, the second-highest-scoring candidate (whether general sound
separation preserves faint bird calls) was dropped because its model
weights and outputs were not accessible.

The divergence repeatedly reached the same technologies and topics,
although no run could see another. AlphaEarth satellite embeddings were
listed in all five runs and used in four of the chosen studies; a
machine-learning weather model (GenCast) was listed in all five, a
time-series foundation model (Chronos) in four, and AlphaFold 3 in four.
Each run’s first “obvious” candidate was about heat, and the last two
chosen studies both used the US National Wetlands Inventory. Within the
procedure, the requirement to use a recent technology with public
outputs and public ground truth narrows the field to a few
well-documented resources.

### 6.3 What the critique changed

The critic raised 21 to 26 points per run, mostly adopted
(Table [4](#S6.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 6.2 Questions the agents formulated ‣ 6 Results ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents")).
It never changed the chosen candidate, but in every run it changed how
the chosen question was compared or measured:

- •
  Run 014: the evaluation moved from the smoothness of embedding
  trajectories to held-out false alarms and misses, with calibration in
  earlier years and testing in later years, and gains were reported
  separately because they were rare.
- •
  Run 015: the decision served by the published summaries was made
  explicit, and the exact distribution of the number of exceeding sites
  became the comparison; the critic pointed out, and the agent accepted,
  that the narrowing of nested bounds is mathematics, not a finding.
- •
  Run 016: the reference data were changed from a classified map to
  farmers’ declarations, because calibrating and validating with the
  same classified map would share its errors; uncertainty and abstention
  became primary endpoints.
- •
  Run 017: inventory boundaries were treated as near-answer information,
  an image-only allocation was added as a control, and the endpoint was
  restricted to the recovery of inventory patches.
- •
  Run 018: the central comparison became the increment of embedding
  distances beyond a strong baseline of public terrain, surface-water
  and drainage covariates; the question was framed as a label-masked
  diagnostic of agreement with inventory classes, not of field
  hydrology.

The agents verified the prior work that the critic cited before using it
and recorded the points they did not adopt, typically new references
they had not checked in full text or proposals for candidates they had
rejected.

Table 5: In-loop review (Claude Opus 5.5 with the run records) of the
first drafts: verdict, scores (1–5) on correctness, verifiability,
novelty, generality, usefulness and clarity, findings by severity, the
agent’s response (adopted + partly adopted), and claims in the final
paper (exploratory in parentheses).

The reviewer re-ran every first draft from its single entry point and
reproduced the reported numbers
(Table [5](#S6.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 6.4 In-loop review and revision ‣ 6 Results ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents"));
verifiability was 5 in all runs. In run 018, for example, the
regenerated paper and claims file were byte-identical to the submitted
ones, and refits of the primary and six control models reproduced the
archived predictions exactly. Four drafts received “major revision” and
one “minor revision”. Novelty (2–3), generality (2) and clarity (2) were
low in all runs.

The leading findings concerned interpretation, not execution. In run
014, the adjustment being tested had little to correct, so its null
effect was largely predictable. In run 015, much of the result followed
from exact moment properties of a 50-member ensemble. In run 016, the
same declaration database served as both truth and audit labels. In run
017, the abstract led with the largest of four split estimates and
omitted planned conditions with different results. In run 018, the only
critical finding of the series: planned null controls (permuted
embeddings, other random seeds) produced changes as large as the real
embeddings, yet the draft’s abstract presented the increment without
applying the qualification rule the agent had itself written before
seeing the results. All 40 findings were adopted (29) or partly adopted
(11). The agents rewrote abstracts around the answer, added the planned
conditions they had omitted, and in run 018 restated the main result as
“an increment attributable to the embeddings was not established”. The
final versions were not reviewed again.

| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 014 | Reference and control corrections of annual-embedding change scores did not consistently improve the screening of one-year tree-cover gains and losses; a directly trained classifier scored higher, with unequal label resources.                                          | Small one-year tests; exploratory changes of the data partition reversed all correction contrasts; performance on the native grid is unverified; multi-year restoration and ecological recovery are not addressed. |
| 015 | Published single-site exceedance probabilities leave wide bounds on the probability that at least $`k`$ of a set of sites exceed a threshold; one aggregate moment narrows them, and all pairwise co-exceedance probabilities nearly determine it.                          | The near-identification is conditional on exact moments of the 50-member empirical forecast law; no observed-weather skill, health benefit or realised economic value was measured.                                |
| 016 | Revisiting the same reference locations gave much smaller errors in the annual change of declared crop-group diversity than independent locations, but predicting no change was better still at every budget; assistance from satellite embeddings gave no or modest gains. | Declaration labels are treated as perfectly repeatable on a fixed frame; field-audit errors, costs and ecological outcomes were not measured.                                                                      |
| 017 | With patch-first allocation of training points, annual embeddings recovered more small inventory wetland patches than seasonal optical imagery in the planned split, but the gain did not transfer reliably between projects.                                               | Intervals exclude the uncertainty of split selection; the endpoint is agreement with the mapped inventory, not ecological completeness or savings in annotation cost.                                              |
| 018 | An increment of embedding distances over terrain, surface-water and drainage covariates for matching wetland water regimes was not established: planned permutation controls gave changes comparable to the real distances.                                                 | Convenience windows; the endpoint is agreement with inventory labels, not field hydroperiod or benefit to practitioners.                                                                                           |

Table 7: External AI evaluation of the final papers (PDF, paper and web

All 20 reviews returned valid output; none reported recognising the
papers. Gemini 4 Argon judged all five papers workshop level, with
overall scores of 5 or 6 (mean 5.4) and main-track judgments of
“borderline” or “no”. Muse Wonder was stricter: overall 3 to 5 (mean
4.1), workshop level “yes” in 3 and “borderline” in 7 of 10 reviews,
main track “no” in all, and two “reject” verdicts (runs 014 and 015).
The two reviewers disagreed most on run 015 (minor revision and 6/10
versus reject or major revision and 4/10). They agreed on the profile:
correctness high (4.4 and 3.8), novelty (3.0 and 2.2), generality (2.6
and 2.0) and clarity (2.3 and 2.0) low, the same profile as the in-loop
reviews. They rated the research questions themselves at 3.2 and 3.4 out
of 5, and in 19 of 20 reviews they judged the main answer “partly”
predictable from the design. Verifiability from the paper alone was
rated 4.3 by Gemini and 2.8 by Muse, below the in-loop 5.0; the in-loop
reviewer had the records, but it was also a different model and reviewed
the first drafts. The two reviews of the same paper differed by 0.4
(Gemini) and 0.6 (Muse) points overall on average.

## 7 Discussion

#### The question can be left to the AI.

With a plain agent, an instruction document and two skills, five
consecutive runs formulated their own questions and carried them through
to revised, re-computable papers without research input from people. The
human set only the area, in one or two sentences; neither the specific
question nor the outputs to report were chosen by people, which makes
the AI’s choices observable.

#### What the AI chose, and what the instructions chose.

Within the technology $`\times`$ societal-problem setting, the agents
chose societal and environmental questions on public data, and the
technology-first procedure pulled them toward a small set of
well-documented resources. The area itself came from the instructions:
in the development runs, the same research model chose caches and
document retrieval when the field was computer science, and societal
problems after one sentence was changed
(Section [4](#S4 "4 Setting the research area: lessons from 13 development runs ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents")).
Within the area, the convergence is partly a property of the procedure
(a recent technology with public outputs and public ground truth) and
partly of the model; we did not vary the model in this series. It
suggests that an AI researcher’s agenda, once the area is set,
concentrates where data and outputs are open. Leaving the question to
the AI therefore does not remove the human choice of area; it makes that
choice small, explicit and testable.

#### Critique and review do different jobs.

The critic, consulted after short feasibility probes but before the main
plan, shaped what was compared and what was claimed; the reviewer, with
the records, checked that the claims followed from the evidence and that
planned analyses were reported. Novelty and generality of the final
papers remained low in both external reviews; since we did not evaluate
the papers before and after the critique and the review, we cannot
estimate how either affected them. The weakest point of the system
remains the choice of a question whose answer matters and is not fixed
by the design.

#### Execution did not limit these runs.

Execution did not prevent completion in these five runs, which chose
their questions partly for feasibility. A separate reviewer agent re-ran
every first draft, and every finding was answered within the response
period. The remaining problems, as in our development runs, were in
framing: which estimate leads the abstract, whether controls are given
their planned weight, and whether the answer was predictable.

#### Future work.

The area setting deserves its own experiments. All five evaluation runs
used one setting, a new technology applied to a societal problem.
Settings other than technology $`\times`$ societal problems remain to be
tested, for example a named scientific field, a given dataset,
theoretical questions, or the open decision of a particular user, as
does a setting with no hint at all, which would separate the effect of
removing the field from that of adding the hint. A more specific setting
may also yield more specific themes, and whether the procedure then
still produces non-obvious questions is open. A human evaluation of the
five papers is planned separately.

## 8 Limitations

Five runs with one research model are a small sample, and we made no
ablation, so we cannot attribute outcomes to the question procedure, the
critic or the reviewer. All evaluations are by AI models; a human
evaluation is planned separately. The in-loop reviewer is from the same
family as the management agent. We counted the pilot run after seeing
three results, and we chose the PDF reviews as the main external result
after seeing the Markdown reviews; both are reported as deviations. The
external reviewers read only the papers, so their verifiability scores
do not reflect the records. Topic selection consulted a critique by
another model, and the hint toward societal problems in the instructions
shaped the domain. The lessons on the area setting
(Section [4](#S4 "4 Setting the research area: lessons from 13 development runs ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents"))
come from development runs in which the research model, its environment
and other parts of the instructions also changed, so they are
observations rather than controlled comparisons. Re-computation by the
reviewer re-ran the agent’s own code on the first draft; it is not an
independent implementation, and it does not establish the correctness of
reference labels or the validity of interpretations. Isolation from
earlier runs relied on separate configuration and on the instructions,
not on access control. The external ratings are uncalibrated AI
judgments of the papers alone. This paper was drafted by the management
agent from the records
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Statement on AI involvement ‣ Letting AI Formulate the Research Question:Autonomous Research Agents")).

## 9 Conclusion

A coding agent given an instruction document and two skills can
formulate its own research question and carry it through to a revised,
verifiable paper, repeatedly and without research input from people. AI
reviewers reading only the papers judged them favourably or borderline
for a workshop in their fields and below the main track, without
calibration against human decisions, and rated their novelty and
generality low. In our development runs, what kind of research resulted
shifted with the one or two sentences that set the research area, and
within that area depended on the procedure that forms the question.
Formulating questions that matter is where autonomous research agents
now need the most work, and leaving the question to them is how to study
it.

#### Availability.

The system (instructions, skills, operating procedure), the five papers
as PDFs with their Markdown sources, the records needed to reproduce
them (plans, events, claims, reviews and responses, code; external data
as retrieval procedures and checksums), and the evaluation scripts are
available at
[https://github.com/kofujimura/autonomous-research-agents](https://github.com/kofujimura/autonomous-research-agents)
(code under the MIT License; text and records under CC BY 4.0;
third-party data under their original terms). The five papers are
attributed to “Autonomous Research Agents”; their wording is unchanged
from the final versions.

## Appendix A External AI evaluation of the Markdown sources

Before the papers were converted to PDF, Gemini 4 Argon reviewed their
Markdown sources with the figures attached as images (same prompt except
for one sentence on the input form; two reviews per paper). The ten
reviews gave mean scores of 4.4 (correctness), 4.3 (verifiability), 2.9
(novelty), 2.7 (generality), 3.4 (usefulness) and 2.4 (clarity), and an
overall score of 5.4, close to the PDF reviews. The prompts, schema,
scripts, raw responses and costs are in the repository.
